items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time”.
items.answer: Weather
items.markingKey: Weather: the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between weather and climate.
items.answer: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere (e.g. today’s rain and temperature); climate is the long-term average pattern of weather, usually over 30 years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a rain gauge is sunk partly into the ground.
items.answer: To stop it being knocked over and to prevent splash from the ground or evaporation from heating, so readings are accurate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stability; 1 mark accuracy [2]

items.stem: A school weather station recorded this data for one week. Maximum temperature (°C): Mon 14, Tue 12, Wed 17, Thu 15, Fri 16, Sat 15, Sun 12. Minimum temperature (°C): Mon 7, Tue 3, Wed 9, Thu 4, Fri 6, Sat 9, Sun 1. Rainfall (mm): Mon 15, Tue 9, Wed 15, Thu 1, Fri 0, Sat 0, Sun 1. (a) Calculate the total rainfall for the week. (b) Describe two ways the students could make their readings more reliable.
items.answer: (a) 41 mm (b) Read the instruments at the same time every day; site them in the open away from buildings; keep the thermometer in a Stevenson screen; continue for longer than one week.

items.stem: How far do you agree that a school weather station can give data that is just as reliable as an official weather station? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: siting; equipment.
items.answer: Agree: Simple instruments (rain gauge, max-min thermometer, anemometer) can be accurate if sited and read correctly. Disagree: School sites are often sheltered by buildings, affecting wind and rain readings. Readings may be missed at weekends and holidays or taken at different times. Official stations use calibrated, automatic equipment and strict siting rules. Judgement: School data can be useful and fairly reliable, but rarely as reliable as official stations without careful siting and routine.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “A north wind blows towards the north.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Winds are named after the direction they blow from, so a north wind blows from the north towards the south.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured in degrees”.

items.markingKey: Latitude: the distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured in degrees. [1]

items.stem: Explain why temperature decreases with altitude.
items.answer: Air is heated mainly from the ground; higher up the air is thinner (lower pressure), holds less heat and is further from the heated surface, so it is colder – about 6.5 °C per 1000 m.
items.markingKey: 1 mark heated from ground; 1 mark thinner air; 1 mark rate [3]

items.stem: Explain why coastal areas have milder winters than inland areas at the same latitude.
items.answer: The sea heats and cools more slowly than land and stores heat from the summer; in winter it releases this heat, warming coastal air.
items.markingKey: 1 mark slow heating/cooling; 1 mark releases heat in winter [2]

items.stem: A town at sea level has an average temperature of 20 °C. A mountain village nearby is at 1500 m. Assume temperature falls by 6.5 °C for every 1000 m. Suggest one way the higher altitude affects farming in the village.
items.answer: Shorter growing season and risk of frost, so farmers grow hardier crops (e.g. potatoes, barley) or keep animals instead of tropical crops.
items.markingKey: 1 mark effect; 1 mark example [2]

items.answer: (a) 11.5 °C (b) The air is heated from the ground; higher air is thinner and further from the warm surface, so it holds less heat.

items.stem: “Latitude is the most important factor affecting the climate of a place.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: prevailing winds; distance from the sea.
items.answer: Agree: Latitude controls the angle of the Sun’s rays and day length, which explains the main pattern of hot equator and cold poles. Disagree: Altitude can override latitude: equatorial mountains such as Kilimanjaro have glaciers. Distance from the sea and ocean currents explain why the UK is milder than places at the same latitude in Canada. Prevailing winds and relief control rainfall. Judgement: Latitude sets the broad pattern, but local factors can be more important for a particular place.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain why tropical rainforest areas have heavy rain almost every afternoon.
items.answer: Intense heating by the high Sun causes moist air to rise (convection), cool and condense, forming towering cumulonimbus clouds and heavy convectional rain.

items.stem: Explain why hot deserts have a very large difference between day and night temperatures.
items.answer: Clear skies let strong sunshine heat the ground by day, and without cloud cover heat escapes quickly at night, so temperatures fall sharply.

items.stem: Mei argues that describing climates using broad zones is too simple to be useful. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement.
items.answer: Agree: Local factors such as altitude, ocean currents and cities create big differences within zones. Zone boundaries are gradual, not sharp lines. Disagree: Zones show the main global patterns clearly and help compare places. They link climate to vegetation and human activity (e.g. farming). Judgement: Zones are a useful starting point but must be combined with local data.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Evaluate the view that human activity is the main cause of climate change today. You may wish to consider: fossil fuels; evidence from data.
items.answer: Agree: CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to over 420 ppm, from burning fossil fuels and deforestation. Warming of about 1.1-1.2 °C since the late 19th century is faster than natural changes. Disagree: Natural factors – Milankovitch cycles, solar variation and volcanic eruptions – have caused big changes in the past. Natural variability (e.g. El Niño) causes short-term ups and downs. Judgement: Natural factors exist, but the evidence strongly shows that human activity is the main cause of current warming.

items.stem: “Mitigation is more important than adaptation in responding to climate change.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: costs; sea defences.
items.answer: Agree: Cutting emissions tackles the cause; without mitigation warming will continue and adaptation will become impossible in some places. Disagree: Some climate change is already happening, so adaptation is needed now to protect lives (sea walls, flood warnings, drought-resistant crops). Poorer countries contributing few emissions need adaptation most. Judgement: Both are essential: mitigation limits future change while adaptation protects people from changes already happening.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “water falling from the atmosphere to the ground as rain, snow, sleet or hail”.
items.answer: Precipitation
items.markingKey: Precipitation: water falling from the atmosphere to the ground as rain, snow, sleet or hail. [1]

items.stem: Explain why weather readings should be taken at the same time each day.
items.answer: Temperature and other elements change through the day, so readings at different times would not be comparable; consistent timing makes the data reliable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark variation through day; 1 mark comparability [2]

items.stem: A school weather station recorded this data for one week. Maximum temperature (°C): Mon 13, Tue 13, Wed 17, Thu 12, Fri 17, Sat 18, Sun 18. Minimum temperature (°C): Mon 9, Tue 3, Wed 9, Thu 8, Fri 11, Sat 11, Sun 13. Rainfall (mm): Mon 15, Tue 12, Wed 9, Thu 2, Fri 4, Sat 15, Sun 4. Name the instrument used to measure each type of data in the table.
items.answer: Maximum-minimum (Six’s) thermometer for temperatures; rain gauge for rainfall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that accurate weather measurement is more important to people today than ever before. You may wish to consider: farming and transport; extreme weather; climate change.
items.answer: Agree: Forecasts protect lives from storms, floods and heatwaves, which are becoming more frequent with climate change. Aviation, shipping, farming and energy supply depend on accurate data. Disagree: People have always depended on the weather, especially farmers in the past. Technology now makes measurement easier, so its importance has not necessarily grown. Judgement: Weather data matters more today because of climate change, global travel and dense populations in hazardous places.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the effect of distance from the sea, giving inland places hotter summers, colder winters and a larger temperature range”.
items.answer: Continentality
items.markingKey: Continentality: the effect of distance from the sea, giving inland places hotter summers, colder winters and a larger temperature range. [1]

items.stem: Explain how ocean currents influence the climate of nearby coasts.
items.answer: Warm currents (e.g. North Atlantic Drift) warm the air above them, giving milder winters and more rain; cold currents (e.g. Humboldt) cool the air, giving cooler, drier conditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark warm; 1 mark cold [2]

items.stem: Two places lie at about 52° N. Place P is on the west coast, facing prevailing westerly winds from the ocean: July average 17 °C, January 8 °C. Place Q is 1500 km inland: July average 23 °C, January -6 °C. Calculate the annual temperature range of P and of Q.
items.answer: P 9 °C; Q 29 °C

items.stem: A town at sea level has an average temperature of 20 °C. A mountain village nearby is at 1500 m. Assume temperature falls by 6.5 °C for every 1000 m. (a) Calculate the expected temperature in the village. (b) Calculate the temperature at a summit 3000 m high.

How far do you agree that latitude is the most important factor affecting the climate of a place? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: distance from the sea; prevailing winds.
items.answer: Agree: Latitude controls the angle of the Sun’s rays and day length, which explains the main pattern of hot equator and cold poles. Disagree: Altitude can override latitude: equatorial mountains such as Kilimanjaro have glaciers. Distance from the sea and ocean currents explain why the UK is milder than places at the same latitude in Canada. Prevailing winds and relief control rainfall. Judgement: Latitude sets the broad pattern, but local factors can be more important for a particular place.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: What is meant by the term “annual temperature range”?
options: The difference between the highest and lowest monthly average temperatures in a year.
A climate that is hot and wet all year, with average temperatures about 27 °C and over 2000 mm of rain.
A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters.
A seasonal reversal of winds that brings a very wet season, as in South Asia from June to September.
items.answer: The difference between the highest and lowest monthly average temperatures in a year.
items.markingKey: Annual temperature range: the difference between the highest and lowest monthly average temperatures in a year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why Mediterranean climates have dry summers.
items.answer: In summer, high pressure (subtropical anticyclones) moves over the region, bringing sinking, dry air and clear skies; in winter it moves south and rain-bearing depressions arrive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark high pressure in summer; 1 mark winter rain [2]

items.stem: Station X: Temperature (°C): Jan 9, Feb 11, Mar 13.5, Apr 14, May 18, Jun 23, Jul 27, Aug 25, Sep 23, Oct 19, Nov 13.5, Dec 10. Precipitation (mm): Jan 50, Feb 40, Mar 35, Apr 30, May 20, Jun 8, Jul 3, Aug 4, Sep 10, Oct 40, Nov 50, Dec 60. Station Y: Temperature (°C): Jan 26, Feb 28, Mar 28.5, Apr 28, May 28, Jun 27.5, Jul 28, Aug 27.5, Sep 28, Oct 26.5, Nov 27, Dec 27. Precipitation (mm): Jan 240, Feb 165, Mar 185, Apr 180, May 170, Jun 160, Jul 155, Aug 170, Sep 165, Oct 190, Nov 255, Dec 290. Compare the total precipitation of X and Y.
items.answer: X 350 mm, Y 2325 mm; Y is wetter by 1975 mm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark totals; 1 mark comparison [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are higher now than at any time in the last 800 000 years.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Ice cores show levels stayed below about 300 ppm over that period; they are now over 420 ppm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the natural and the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.answer: The natural effect is caused by gases that have always been present and keeps Earth about 33 °C warmer; the enhanced effect is caused by extra gases from human activity, trapping more heat and causing global warming.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each; 1 mark contrast [3]

items.stem: Annual average carbon dioxide concentration measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (parts per million): 1960: 317, 1970: 326, 1980: 339, 1990: 354, 2000: 370, 2010: 390, 2020: 414. Suggest why the measurements are taken on Mauna Loa, Hawaii.
items.answer: It is high and far from cities and large sources of pollution, so measurements represent well-mixed global air.
items.markingKey: 1 mark remote; 1 mark representative [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that human activity is the main cause of climate change today. You may wish to consider: natural causes; evidence from data.
items.answer: Agree: CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to over 420 ppm, from burning fossil fuels and deforestation. Warming of about 1.1-1.2 °C since the late 19th century is faster than natural changes. Disagree: Natural factors – Milankovitch cycles, solar variation and volcanic eruptions – have caused big changes in the past. Natural variability (e.g. El Niño) causes short-term ups and downs. Judgement: Natural factors exist, but the evidence strongly shows that human activity is the main cause of current warming.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: “Human activity is the main cause of climate change today.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: evidence from data; deforestation.

Warming of about 1.1-1.2 °C since the late 19th century is faster than natural changes. Disagree: Natural factors – Milankovitch cycles, solar variation and volcanic eruptions – have caused big changes in the past. Natural variability (e.g. El Niño) causes short-term ups and downs. Judgement: Natural factors exist, but the evidence strongly shows that human activity is the main cause of current warming.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “Melting sea ice in the Arctic is the main cause of sea-level rise.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water; melting land ice (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctica) and thermal expansion cause sea-level rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Global sea level is currently rising by about 3.3 mm per year. The lowest homes on a coastal town in the Netherlands are about 120 cm above high tide. Explain why this is an issue of fairness between countries.
items.answer: Low-lying and poorer countries have produced very small emissions but face the worst impacts, while richer countries produced most past emissions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark low emissions/high impacts; 1 mark rich countries responsible [2]

items.stem: Global sea level is currently rising by about 3.7 mm per year. The lowest homes on an island in the Maldives are about 50 cm above high tide. (a) Calculate the rise in sea level in 75 years, in centimetres. (b) Calculate how far above high tide the lowest homes would then be.
